question: Find the LCM and HCF of the following pairs of integers and verify that LCM × HCF = product of the two numbers: (i) 26 and 91 (ii) 510 and 92 (iii) 336 and 54
steps: Prime-factorise both numbers first
HCF = product of the smallest power of each COMMON prime; LCM = product of the greatest power of every prime that appears
Verify by checking HCF × LCM equals the product of the original two numbers

question: Find the LCM and HCF of the following integers by applying the prime factorisation method: (i) 12, 15 and 21 (ii) 17, 23 and 29 (iii) 8, 9 and 25
solution:
(i) 12 = 2²×3, 15 = 3×5, 21 = 3×7. HCF = 3, LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.
(ii) 17, 23, 29 are all primes with no common factor. HCF = 1, LCM = 17×23×29 = 11339.
(iii) 8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 25 = 5². No common prime factor. HCF = 1, LCM = 2³×3²×5² = 1800.
steps: Prime-factorise all three numbers
HCF = smallest power of any prime common to ALL of them (1 if none is common to all three)
LCM = product of the greatest power of every prime appearing in any of the numbers

question: Given that HCF (306, 657) = 9, find LCM (306, 657).
solution: For any two positive integers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers. So LCM = (306 × 657) ÷ 9 = 201042 ÷ 9 = 22338.
steps: Use the identity HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b

question: Check whether 6ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.
solution: 6ⁿ = (2×3)ⁿ = 2ⁿ×3ⁿ. For a number to end in 0, it must be divisible by 10 = 2×5, so its prime factorisation must include both 2 and 5. But the only prime factors of 6ⁿ are 2 and 3 — 5 never appears, no matter what n is. So 6ⁿ can never end with the digit 0.
steps: Ending in 0 means the number is divisible by 10 = 2 × 5
Prime-factorise 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ — its only prime factors are 2 and 3
Since 5 is never a factor of 6ⁿ, it can never end in 0 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees uniqueness of prime factors)

question: Explain why 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 and 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 5 are composite numbers.
solution:
7×11×13 + 13 = 13×(7×11 + 1) = 13×78 = 13×2×3×13. This is a product of factors other than 1 and itself, so it is composite.
7×6×5×4×3×2×1 + 5 = 5040 + 5 = 5045 = 5×(1008 + 1) = 5×1009. Since it can be written as a product of two integers greater than 1 (5 and 1009), it is composite.
steps: Factor out the common term 13 from the first expression: 13×(7×11+1) = 13×78
Factor out the common term 5 from the second expression: 5×(1008+1) = 5×1009
Any number expressible as a product of two integers greater than 1 is, by definition, composite

question: There is a circular path around a sports field. Sonia takes 18 minutes to drive one round of the field, while Ravi takes 12 minutes for the same. Suppose they both start at the same point and at the same time, and go in the same direction. After how many minutes will they meet again at the starting point?
solution: They will next be together at the starting point after LCM(18, 12) minutes. 18 = 2×3², 12 = 2²×3, so LCM = 2²×3² = 36. They will meet again at the starting point after 36 minutes.
steps: The time to meet again at the START is the LCM of their individual lap times, not the HCF
LCM = 2²×3² = 36 minutes

question: Prove that √5 is irrational.
solution: Assume, to the contrary, that √5 is rational. Then √5 = a/b for coprime integers a, b (b≠0). Squaring: 5b² = a², so 5 divides a², and hence 5 divides a. Write a = 5c. Substituting: 5b² = 25c², so b² = 5c², which means 5 divides b² and hence 5 divides b. But then 5 divides both a and b, contradicting that they are coprime. This contradiction shows our assumption was wrong, so √5 is irrational.
steps: Assume √5 = a/b in lowest terms (a, b coprime), for contradiction
Show 5 | a² ⟹ 5 | a, substitute a = 5c
Show this forces 5 | b too — contradicting that a, b share no common factor

question: Prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational.
solution: Assume, to the contrary, that 3 + 2√5 is rational. Then 3 + 2√5 = a/b for some integers a, b (b≠0). Rearranging: 2√5 = a/b − 3, so √5 = (a − 3b)/(2b). Since a and b are integers, the right-hand side is a ratio of integers, i.e. a rational number. But this contradicts the fact that √5 is irrational. Hence 3 + 2√5 is irrational.
steps: Assume 3 + 2√5 = a/b is rational, for contradiction
Isolate √5: √5 = (a − 3b)/(2b), a ratio of integers
This would make √5 rational, contradicting the known fact that √5 is irrational

question: Prove that the following are irrationals: (i) 1/√2 (ii) 7√5 (iii) 6 + √2
solution:
(i) If 1/√2 = a/b were rational, then √2 = b/a would also be rational — contradicting that √2 is irrational. So 1/√2 is irrational.
(ii) If 7√5 = a/b were rational, then √5 = a/(7b) would be a ratio of integers, i.e. rational — contradicting that √5 is irrational. So 7√5 is irrational.
(iii) If 6 + √2 = a/b were rational, then √2 = a/b − 6 = (a−6b)/b would be rational — contradicting that √2 is irrational. So 6 + √2 is irrational.
steps: In each case, assume the expression is rational (equal to a/b) and rearrange to isolate the known irrational (√2 or √5)
The rearranged form is always a ratio of integers, i.e. rational
This contradicts the known irrationality of √2/√5, so the original expression must be irrational

question: Find the zeroes of the following quadratic polynomials and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients: (i) x² – 2x – 8 (ii) 4s² – 4s + 1 (iii) 6x² – 3 – 7x (iv) 4u² + 8u (v) t² – 15 (vi) 3x² – x – 4
steps: Factorise each quadratic by splitting the middle term
Set each factor to zero to get the two zeroes
Check sum of zeroes = –b/a and product of zeroes = c/a in every case

question: Find a quadratic polynomial each with the given numbers as the sum and product of its zeroes respectively: (i) 1/4, –1 (ii) √2, 1/3 (iii) 0, √5 (iv) 1, 1 (v) –1/4, 1/4 (vi) 4, 1
solution:
A quadratic polynomial with sum of zeroes S and product of zeroes P is k[x² – Sx + P], for any nonzero constant k. Taking k = 1 (or a convenient value to clear fractions):

(i) S = 1/4, P = –1 → x² – (1/4)x – 1. Multiplying by 4: 4x² – x – 4.
(ii) S = √2, P = 1/3 → x² – √2x + 1/3. Multiplying by 3: 3x² – 3√2x + 1.
(iii) S = 0, P = √5 → x² + √5.
(iv) S = 1, P = 1 → x² – x + 1.
(v) S = –1/4, P = 1/4 → x² + (1/4)x + 1/4. Multiplying by 4: 4x² + x + 1.
(vi) S = 4, P = 1 → x² – 4x + 1.
steps: Use the general form x² – (sum)x + (product) for the required polynomial
Multiply through by a suitable constant to clear fractions where convenient
Any constant multiple of the polynomial found is also a valid answer

question: Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions: (i) 10 students of Class X took part in a Mathematics quiz. If the number of girls is 4 more than the number of boys, find the number of boys and girls who took part in the quiz. (ii) 5 pencils and 7 pens together cost ₹50, whereas 7 pencils and 5 pens together cost ₹46. Find the cost of one pencil and that of one pen.
solution:
(i) Let the number of boys = x and number of girls = y.
x + y = 10 ... (1)
y = x + 4, i.e., y – x = 4 ... (2)
Adding (1) and (2) after rewriting (1) as –x + y = ... ; instead add (1) and (2) directly: from (2), y = x + 4. Substitute in (1): x + (x + 4) = 10 → 2x = 6 → x = 3, y = 7.
So there are 3 boys and 7 girls.

(ii) Let the cost of a pencil = ₹x and cost of a pen = ₹y.
5x + 7y = 50 ... (1)
7x + 5y = 46 ... (2)
Adding (1) and (2): 12x + 12y = 96 → x + y = 8 ... (3)
Subtracting (2) from (1): –2x + 2y = 4 → –x + y = 2 ... (4)
Adding (3) and (4): 2y = 10 → y = 5, then x = 3.
So the cost of a pencil is ₹3 and the cost of a pen is ₹5.
steps: Translate each word problem into two linear equations in two variables
(i) Use x+y=10 and y–x=4 to get x=3, y=7
(ii) Add and subtract the two cost equations to solve x=3, y=5

question: On comparing the ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂ and c₁/c₂, find out whether the lines representing the following pairs of linear equations intersect at a point, are parallel or coincident: (i) 5x – 4y + 8 = 0; 7x + 6y – 9 = 0 (ii) 9x + 3y + 12 = 0; 18x + 6y + 24 = 0 (iii) 6x – 3y + 10 = 0; 2x – y + 9 = 0
solution:
(i) a₁/a₂ = 5/7, b₁/b₂ = –4/6 = –2/3. Since 5/7 ≠ –2/3, the lines intersect at a point.

(ii) a₁/a₂ = 9/18 = 1/2, b₁/b₂ = 3/6 = 1/2, c₁/c₂ = 12/24 = 1/2. Since a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ = 1/2, the lines are coincident.

(iii) a₁/a₂ = 6/2 = 3, b₁/b₂ = –3/–1 = 3, c₁/c₂ = 10/9. Since a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = 3 ≠ 10/9 = c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel.
steps: Write each pair as a₁x+b₁y+c₁=0 and a₂x+b₂y+c₂=0
Compare a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂: all different → intersecting; all equal → coincident; first two equal but third different → parallel
(i) intersecting (ii) coincident (iii) parallel

question: On comparing the ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂ and c₁/c₂, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent: (i) 3x + 2y = 5; 2x – 3y = 7 (ii) 2x – 3y = 8; 4x – 6y = 9 (iii) (3/2)x + (5/3)y = 7; 9x – 10y = 14 (iv) 5x – 3y = 11; –10x + 6y = –22 (v) (4/3)x + 2y = 8; 2x + 3y = 12
solution:
(i) a₁/a₂ = 3/2, b₁/b₂ = 2/–3. Since 3/2 ≠ –2/3, the lines intersect → consistent (unique solution).

(ii) a₁/a₂ = 2/4 = 1/2, b₁/b₂ = –3/–6 = 1/2, c₁/c₂ = 8/9. Since a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel → inconsistent (no solution).

(iii) a₁/a₂ = (3/2)/9 = 1/6, b₁/b₂ = (5/3)/(–10) = –1/6. Since 1/6 ≠ –1/6, consistent (unique solution).

(iv) a₁/a₂ = 5/–10 = –1/2, b₁/b₂ = –3/6 = –1/2, c₁/c₂ = 11/–22 = –1/2. All three equal → coincident lines → consistent (infinitely many solutions).

(v) a₁/a₂ = (4/3)/2 = 2/3, b₁/b₂ = 2/3, c₁/c₂ = 8/12 = 2/3. All three equal → coincident lines → consistent (infinitely many solutions).
steps: Compare a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂ for each pair
Different ratios → consistent; equal first two but unequal third → inconsistent; all equal → consistent (infinite solutions)
(i) consistent (ii) inconsistent (iii) consistent (iv) consistent, infinite solutions (v) consistent, infinite solutions

chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
question: Which of the following pairs of linear equations are consistent/inconsistent? If consistent, obtain the solution: (i) x + y = 5, 2x + 2y = 10 (ii) x – y = 8, 3x – 3y = 16 (iii) 2x + y – 6 = 0, 4x – 2y – 4 = 0 (iv) 2x – 2y – 2 = 0, 4x – 4y – 5 = 0
solution:
(i) a₁/a₂ = 1/2, b₁/b₂ = 1/2, c₁/c₂ = 5/10 = 1/2. All equal → coincident → consistent, with infinitely many solutions (every point satisfying x + y = 5).

(ii) a₁/a₂ = 1/3, b₁/b₂ = –1/–3 = 1/3, c₁/c₂ = 8/16 = 1/2. First two ratios equal but not the third → parallel lines → inconsistent (no solution).

(iii) a₁/a₂ = 2/4 = 1/2, b₁/b₂ = 1/–2 = –1/2. Since 1/2 ≠ –1/2, lines intersect → consistent. Solve: 2x + y = 6 and 4x – 2y = 4, i.e., 2x – y = 2. Adding: 4x = 8 → x = 2, then y = 6 – 4 = 2. Solution: x = 2, y = 2.

(iv) a₁/a₂ = 2/4 = 1/2, b₁/b₂ = –2/–4 = 1/2, c₁/c₂ = –2/–5 = 2/5. First two equal but not the third → parallel → inconsistent (no solution).
steps: Check ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂ to classify each pair
(i) infinite solutions (ii) no solution (iii) unique solution x=2, y=2 (iv) no solution
For (iii), solve by elimination: add the equations to eliminate y

question: Half the perimeter of a rectangular garden, whose length is 4 m more than its width, is 36 m. Find the dimensions of the garden.
solution:
Let the width = x m and length = y m.
Given: y = x + 4 ... (1)
Half the perimeter = x + y = 36 ... (2)
Substituting (1) in (2): x + (x + 4) = 36 → 2x = 32 → x = 16.
Then y = 16 + 4 = 20.
So the width of the garden is 16 m and the length is 20 m.
steps: Let width = x, length = y; form y = x+4 and x+y=36
Substitute to solve: 2x+4=36 → x=16
Width = 16 m, Length = 20 m

question: Given the linear equation 2x + 3y – 8 = 0, write another linear equation in two variables such that the geometrical representation of the pair so formed is: (i) intersecting lines (ii) parallel lines (iii) coincident lines
solution:
For 2x + 3y – 8 = 0, we have a₁ = 2, b₁ = 3, c₁ = –8.

(i) Intersecting lines: choose a₂/a₁ ≠ b₂/b₁, e.g., 3x + 2y – 7 = 0 (ratio 3/2 ≠ 2/3).

(ii) Parallel lines: choose a₂/a₁ = b₂/b₁ ≠ c₂/c₁, e.g., 4x + 6y – 5 = 0 (ratios 4/2 = 6/3 = 2, but –5/–8 ≠ 2).

(iii) Coincident lines: choose a₂/a₁ = b₂/b₁ = c₂/c₁, e.g., 4x + 6y – 16 = 0 (all ratios equal to 2, since it is just 2 × (original equation)).
steps: Use ratio conditions on a,b,c between the two equations
Different a:b ratio → intersecting; equal a:b but different c ratio → parallel; all equal → coincident
Example answers: 3x+2y-7=0 (intersecting), 4x+6y-5=0 (parallel), 4x+6y-16=0 (coincident)

question: Draw the graphs of the equations x – y + 1 = 0 and 3x + 2y – 12 = 0. Determine the coordinates of the vertices of the triangle formed by these lines and the x-axis, and shade the triangular region.
solution:
The triangle is formed by the two given lines and the x-axis, so its vertices are: the point where each line meets the x-axis, and the point where the two lines meet each other.

x – y + 1 = 0 meets the x-axis (y = 0): x + 1 = 0 → x = –1. So one vertex is (–1, 0).

3x + 2y – 12 = 0 meets the x-axis (y = 0): 3x = 12 → x = 4. So another vertex is (4, 0).

Intersection of the two lines: from x – y + 1 = 0, y = x + 1. Substitute in 3x + 2y – 12 = 0: 3x + 2(x + 1) – 12 = 0 → 5x – 10 = 0 → x = 2, then y = 3. So the third vertex is (2, 3).

Therefore, the triangle formed has vertices (–1, 0), (4, 0) and (2, 3). (The triangular region enclosed by the two lines and the x-axis, with these vertices, is the shaded region.)
steps: Find where each line crosses the x-axis (set y=0)
Find the intersection point of the two lines by solving them together
Vertices of the triangle: (–1,0), (4,0), (2,3)

question: Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method: (i) x + y = 14, x – y = 4 (ii) s – t = 3, s/3 + t/2 = 6 (iii) 3x – y = 3, 9x – 3y = 9 (iv) 0.2x + 0.3y = 1.3, 0.4x + 0.5y = 2.3 (v) √2x + √3y = 0, √3x – √8y = 0 (vi) (3x/2) – (5y/3) = –2, x/3 + y/2 = 13/6
solution:
(i) From x + y = 14, x = 14 – y. Substitute in x – y = 4: (14 – y) – y = 4 → 14 – 2y = 4 → y = 5. Then x = 9.
Solution: x = 9, y = 5.

(ii) From s – t = 3, s = t + 3. Substitute in s/3 + t/2 = 6: (t+3)/3 + t/2 = 6. Multiply by 6: 2(t+3) + 3t = 36 → 2t + 6 + 3t = 36 → 5t = 30 → t = 6. Then s = 9.
Solution: s = 9, t = 6.

(iii) From 3x – y = 3, y = 3x – 3. Substitute in 9x – 3y = 9: 9x – 3(3x – 3) = 9 → 9x – 9x + 9 = 9 → 9 = 9, true for all x. So the equations are dependent — there are infinitely many solutions (the two equations represent the same line).

(iv) From 0.2x + 0.3y = 1.3, multiply by 10: 2x + 3y = 13, so x = (13 – 3y)/2. Substitute in 0.4x + 0.5y = 2.3 (×10: 4x + 5y = 23): 4×(13–3y)/2 + 5y = 23 → 2(13–3y) + 5y = 23 → 26 – 6y + 5y = 23 → 26 – y = 23 → y = 3. Then x = (13–9)/2 = 2.
Solution: x = 2, y = 3.

(v) From √2x + √3y = 0, x = –√3y/√2. Substitute in √3x – √8y = 0: √3(–√3y/√2) – √8y = 0 → –3y/√2 – 2√2y = 0 → y(–3/√2 – 2√2) = 0 → y = 0 (since the coefficient is nonzero). Then x = 0.
Solution: x = 0, y = 0.

(vi) From x/3 + y/2 = 13/6, multiply by 6: 2x + 3y = 13, so x = (13 – 3y)/2. Substitute in (3x/2) – (5y/3) = –2 (multiply this by 6: 9x – 10y = –12): 9×(13–3y)/2 – 10y = –12 → 9(13–3y) – 20y = –24 → 117 – 27y – 20y = –24 → 117 – 47y = –24 → 47y = 141 → y = 3. Then x = (13–9)/2 = 2.
Solution: x = 2, y = 3.
steps: Express one variable in terms of the other from the simpler equation
Substitute into the second equation and solve for the remaining variable
(i) x=9,y=5 (ii) s=9,t=6 (iii) infinite solutions (iv) x=2,y=3 (v) x=0,y=0 (vi) x=2,y=3

question: Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method: (i) The difference between two numbers is 26 and one number is three times the other. Find them. (ii) The larger of two supplementary angles exceeds the smaller by 18 degrees. Find them. (iii) The coach of a cricket team buys 7 bats and 6 balls for ₹3800. Later, she buys 3 bats and 5 balls for ₹1750. Find the cost of each bat and each ball. (iv) The taxi charges in a city consist of a fixed charge together with the charge for the distance covered. For a distance of 10 km, the charge paid is ₹105 and for a journey of 15 km, the charge paid is ₹155. What are the fixed charges and the charge per km? How much does a person have to pay for travelling a distance of 25 km? (v) A fraction becomes 9/11, if 2 is added to both the numerator and the denominator. If 3 is added to both the numerator and the denominator it becomes 5/6. Find the fraction. (vi) Five years hence, the age of Jacob will be three times that of his son. Five years ago, Jacob's age was seven times that of his son. What are their present ages?
solution:
(i) Let the larger number = x, smaller = y. x – y = 26 ... (1), x = 3y ... (2).
Substitute (2) in (1): 3y – y = 26 → 2y = 26 → y = 13, x = 39.
The numbers are 39 and 13.

(ii) Let the larger angle = x, smaller = y. x + y = 180 (supplementary) ... (1), x – y = 18 ... (2), so x = y + 18.
Substitute in (1): (y + 18) + y = 180 → 2y = 162 → y = 81, x = 99.
The angles are 99° and 81°.

(iii) Let cost of a bat = ₹x, a ball = ₹y.
7x + 6y = 3800 ... (1)
3x + 5y = 1750 ... (2)
From (2): x = (1750 – 5y)/3. Substitute in (1): 7(1750–5y)/3 + 6y = 3800 → 7(1750–5y) + 18y = 11400 → 12250 – 35y + 18y = 11400 → 12250 – 17y = 11400 → 17y = 850 → y = 50. Then x = (1750–250)/3 = 1500/3 = 500.
Cost of a bat = ₹500, cost of a ball = ₹50.

(iv) Let fixed charge = ₹x, charge per km = ₹y.
x + 10y = 105 ... (1)
x + 15y = 155 ... (2)
Subtracting (1) from (2): 5y = 50 → y = 10. Then x = 105 – 100 = 5.
Fixed charge = ₹5, charge per km = ₹10.
For 25 km: charge = 5 + 25×10 = ₹255.

(v) Let the fraction be x/y.
(x+2)/(y+2) = 9/11 → 11(x+2) = 9(y+2) → 11x + 22 = 9y + 18 → 11x – 9y = –4 ... (1)
(x+3)/(y+3) = 5/6 → 6(x+3) = 5(y+3) → 6x + 18 = 5y + 15 → 6x – 5y = –3 ... (2)
From (1): x = (9y – 4)/11. Substitute in (2): 6(9y–4)/11 – 5y = –3 → 6(9y–4) – 55y = –33 → 54y – 24 – 55y = –33 → –y – 24 = –33 → y = 9. Then x = (81–4)/11 = 77/11 = 7.
The fraction is 7/9.

(vi) Let Jacob's present age = x years and his son's present age = y years.
Five years hence: x + 5 = 3(y + 5) → x + 5 = 3y + 15 → x – 3y = 10 ... (1)
Five years ago: x – 5 = 7(y – 5) → x – 5 = 7y – 35 → x – 7y = –30 ... (2)
Subtracting (2) from (1): 4y = 40 → y = 10. Then x = 10 + 30 = 40.
Jacob's present age is 40 years and his son's present age is 10 years.
steps: Translate each scenario into a pair of linear equations
Use substitution to solve for both unknowns in each part
(i) 39,13 (ii) 99°,81° (iii) bat ₹500, ball ₹50 (iv) fixed ₹5, per km ₹10, 25km→₹255 (v) fraction 7/9 (vi) Jacob 40, son 10

question: Solve the following pair of linear equations by the elimination method and the substitution method: (i) x + y = 5 and 2x – 3y = 4 (ii) 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x – 2y = 2 (iii) 3x – 5y – 4 = 0 and 9x = 2y + 7 (iv) x/2 + 2y/3 = –1 and x – y/3 = 3
solution:
(i) Elimination: from x + y = 5, multiply by 3: 3x + 3y = 15. Add to 2x – 3y = 4: 5x = 19 → x = 19/5. Then y = 5 – 19/5 = 6/5.
Substitution check: y = 5 – x, substitute into 2x – 3(5–x) = 4 → 2x – 15 + 3x = 4 → 5x = 19 → x = 19/5, y = 6/5. Same answer.
Solution: x = 19/5, y = 6/5.

(ii) Elimination: 3x + 4y = 10 ... (1); 2x – 2y = 2 → x – y = 1 ... (2). Multiply (2) by 4: 4x – 4y = 4. Multiply (1) by 1 and add appropriately: multiply (2) by 2: 2x – 2y = 2 (already given). Instead, multiply (1) by 1 and (2) by 2: 2x-2y=2 already; add (1) and 2×(2): (3x+4y) + (4x - 4y)=10+4 → 7x = 14 → x = 2. From (2): y = x – 1 = 1.
Solution: x = 2, y = 1.

(iii) 3x – 5y = 4 ... (1); 9x – 2y = 7 ... (2). Multiply (1) by 3: 9x – 15y = 12. Subtract (2): (9x–15y)–(9x–2y) = 12–7 → –13y = 5 → y = –5/13. From (1): 3x = 4 + 5y = 4 – 25/13 = (52–25)/13 = 27/13 → x = 9/13.
Solution: x = 9/13, y = –5/13.

(iv) Multiply x/2 + 2y/3 = –1 by 6: 3x + 4y = –6 ... (1). Multiply x – y/3 = 3 by 3: 3x – y = 9 ... (2). Subtract (2) from (1): 5y = –15 → y = –3. From (2): 3x = 9 + y = 9 – 3 = 6 → x = 2.
Solution: x = 2, y = –3.

chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
question: Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method: (i) If we add 1 to the numerator and subtract 1 from the denominator, a fraction reduces to 1. It becomes 1/2 if we only add 1 to the denominator. What is the fraction? (ii) Five years ago, Nuri was thrice as old as Sonu. Ten years later, Nuri will be twice as old as Sonu. How old are Nuri and Sonu? (iii) The sum of the digits of a two-digit number is 9. Also, nine times this number is twice the number obtained by reversing the order of the digits. Find the number. (iv) Meena went to a bank to withdraw ₹2000. She asked the cashier to give her ₹50 and ₹100 notes only. Meena got 25 notes in all. Find how many notes of ₹50 and ₹100 she received. (v) A lending library has a fixed charge for the first three days and an additional charge for each day thereafter. Saritha paid ₹27 for a book kept for seven days, while Susy paid ₹21 for the book she kept for five days. Find the fixed charge and the charge for each extra day.
solution:
(i) Let the fraction be x/y.
(x+1)/(y–1) = 1 → x + 1 = y – 1 → x – y = –2 ... (1)
x/(y+1) = 1/2 → 2x = y + 1 → 2x – y = 1 ... (2)
Subtract (1) from (2): (2x–y) – (x–y) = 1–(–2) → x = 3. From (1): 3 – y = –2 → y = 5.
The fraction is 3/5.

(ii) Let Nuri's present age = x, Sonu's = y.
Five years ago: x – 5 = 3(y – 5) → x – 3y = –10 ... (1)
Ten years later: x + 10 = 2(y + 10) → x – 2y = 10 ... (2)
Subtract (1) from (2): y = 20. From (2): x = 10 + 40 = 50.
Nuri is 50 years old and Sonu is 20 years old.

(iii) Let tens digit = x, units digit = y. Number = 10x + y.
x + y = 9 ... (1)
9(10x + y) = 2(10y + x) → 90x + 9y = 20y + 2x → 88x = 11y → y = 8x ... (2)
Substitute in (1): x + 8x = 9 → 9x = 9 → x = 1, y = 8.
The number is 18.

(iv) Let number of ₹50 notes = x, ₹100 notes = y.
x + y = 25 ... (1)
50x + 100y = 2000 → x + 2y = 40 ... (2)
Subtract (1) from (2): y = 15. From (1): x = 10.
Meena received 10 notes of ₹50 and 15 notes of ₹100.

(v) Let fixed charge for first 3 days = ₹x, additional charge per day thereafter = ₹y.
Saritha (7 days, 4 extra days): x + 4y = 27 ... (1)
Susy (5 days, 2 extra days): x + 2y = 21 ... (2)
Subtract (2) from (1): 2y = 6 → y = 3. From (2): x = 21 – 6 = 15.
Fixed charge = ₹15, additional charge per day = ₹3.
steps: Set up two linear equations from each real-world condition
Eliminate one variable by subtraction after matching coefficients
(i) 3/5 (ii) Nuri 50, Sonu 20 (iii) 18 (iv) 10 fifty-notes, 15 hundred-notes (v) fixed ₹15, extra ₹3/day

question: Check whether the following are quadratic equations: (i) (x+1)² = 2(x–3) (ii) x² – 2x = (–2)(3–x) (iii) (x–2)(x+1) = (x–1)(x+3) (iv) (x–3)(2x+1) = x(x+5) (v) (2x–1)(x–3) = (x+5)(x–1) (vi) x² + 3x + 1 = (x–2)² (vii) (x+2)³ = 2x(x²–1) (viii) x³ – 4x² – x + 1 = (x–2)³
solution:
(i) LHS = x² + 2x + 1, RHS = 2x – 6. Equation: x² + 2x + 1 – 2x + 6 = 0 → x² + 7 = 0. This is of the form ax²+bx+c=0 (a=1≠0). Quadratic equation.

(ii) LHS = x² – 2x, RHS = –6 + 2x. Equation: x² – 2x + 6 – 2x = 0 → x² – 4x + 6 = 0. Quadratic equation.

(iii) LHS = x² – x – 2, RHS = x² + 2x – 3. Equation: (x²–x–2) – (x²+2x–3) = 0 → –3x + 1 = 0. Not of the form ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0 — it's linear. Not a quadratic equation.

(iv) LHS = 2x² – 5x – 3, RHS = x² + 5x. Equation: 2x²–5x–3–x²–5x=0 → x² – 10x – 3 = 0. Quadratic equation.

(v) LHS = 2x² – 7x + 3, RHS = x² + 4x – 5. Equation: 2x²–7x+3–x²–4x+5=0 → x² – 11x + 8 = 0. Quadratic equation.

(vi) LHS = x²+3x+1, RHS = x² – 4x + 4. Equation: x²+3x+1–x²+4x–4=0 → 7x – 3 = 0. Linear, not quadratic equation.

(vii) LHS = x³+6x²+12x+8, RHS = 2x³–2x. Equation: x³+6x²+12x+8–2x³+2x=0 → –x³+6x²+14x+8=0, i.e. x³–6x²–14x–8=0. This is a cubic equation, not quadratic.

(viii) LHS = x³–4x²–x+1, RHS = x³–6x²+12x–8. Equation: (x³–4x²–x+1)–(x³–6x²+12x–8)=0 → 2x²–13x+9=0. Quadratic equation.
steps: Expand both sides fully and bring all terms to one side
It's a quadratic equation only if the simplified form is ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0
Quadratic: (i),(ii),(iv),(v),(viii). Not quadratic: (iii) linear, (vi) linear, (vii) cubic

question: Represent the following situations in the form of quadratic equations: (i) The area of a rectangular plot is 528 m². The length of the plot (in metres) is one more than twice its breadth. We need to find the length and breadth of the plot. (ii) The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306. We need to find the integers. (iii) Rohan's mother is 26 years older than him. The product of their ages (in years) 3 years from now will be 360. We would like to find Rohan's present age. (iv) A train travels a distance of 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 8 km/h less, then it would have taken 3 hours more to cover the same distance. We need to find the speed of the train.
solution:
(i) Let the breadth = x m. Then the length = (2x + 1) m.
Area = length × breadth: (2x+1)x = 528 → 2x² + x – 528 = 0.

(ii) Let the smaller integer = x. Then the next consecutive integer = x + 1.
Product: x(x+1) = 306 → x² + x – 306 = 0.

(iii) Let Rohan's present age = x years. His mother's present age = x + 26.
Three years from now: Rohan's age = x + 3, mother's age = x + 29.
Product = 360: (x+3)(x+29) = 360 → x² + 32x + 87 = 360 → x² + 32x – 273 = 0.

(iv) Let the speed of the train = x km/h. Time taken = 480/x hours.
If speed is (x – 8) km/h, time taken = 480/(x–8) hours, which is 3 hours more:
480/(x–8) – 480/x = 3
Multiply through by x(x–8): 480x – 480(x–8) = 3x(x–8)
480x – 480x + 3840 = 3x² – 24x
3840 = 3x² – 24x
Divide by 3: x² – 8x – 1280 = 0.
steps: Assign a variable to the unknown quantity and express related quantities in terms of it
Use the given product/area/time relationship to form an equation

question: Solve the problems given in Example 1: (i) John and Jivanti together have 45 marbles. Both of them lost 5 marbles each, and the product of the number of marbles they now have is 124. Find how many marbles they had to start with. (ii) A cottage industry produces a certain number of toys in a day. The cost of production of each toy (in rupees) was found to be 55 minus the number of toys produced in a day. On a particular day, the total cost of production was ₹750. Find the number of toys produced on that day.
solution:
(i) Let John's marbles = x, so Jivanti's = 45 – x. After losing 5 each: John has (x–5), Jivanti has (40–x).
Given product = 124: (x–5)(40–x) = 124 → 40x – x² – 200 + 5x = 124 → –x² + 45x – 200 = 124 → x² – 45x + 324 = 0.
Factorising: we need two numbers with sum 45 and product 324 → 36 and 9. So (x–36)(x–9) = 0 → x = 36 or x = 9.
If John had 36, Jivanti had 9 (or vice-versa). Both are valid, so John and Jivanti had 36 and 9 marbles (in either order) to start with.

(ii) Let the number of toys = x. Cost per toy = 55 – x. Total cost: x(55–x) = 750 → 55x – x² = 750 → x² – 55x + 750 = 0.
Factorising: two numbers with sum 55, product 750 → 25 and 30. (x–25)(x–30) = 0 → x = 25 or x = 30.
So 25 or 30 toys were produced on that day (both values satisfy the conditions).
steps: Translate each situation into a quadratic equation, as done in Example 1 of the chapter
Factorise by finding two numbers with the required sum and product
(i) 36 and 9 marbles (ii) 25 or 30 toys

question: Find two numbers whose sum is 27 and product is 182.
solution:
Let one number = x, the other = 27 – x.
Product: x(27–x) = 182 → 27x – x² = 182 → x² – 27x + 182 = 0.
Discriminant = 27² – 4×182 = 729 – 728 = 1. √1 = 1.
x = (27 ± 1)/2 = 14 or 13.
So the two numbers are 13 and 14.
steps: Let numbers be x and 27–x, form x²-27x+182=0
Solve using the quadratic formula (discriminant = 1)
Numbers are 13 and 14

question: Find two consecutive positive integers, sum of whose squares is 365.
solution:
Let the integers be x and x+1.
x² + (x+1)² = 365 → x² + x² + 2x + 1 = 365 → 2x² + 2x – 364 = 0 → x² + x – 182 = 0.
Discriminant = 1 + 728 = 729, √729 = 27.
x = (–1 ± 27)/2 = 13 or –14.
Since the integers must be positive, x = 13, and the other integer is 14.
The two consecutive positive integers are 13 and 14.
steps: Let integers be x, x+1; form x²+x-182=0
Solve using the quadratic formula, discarding the negative root
The integers are 13 and 14

question: The altitude of a right triangle is 7 cm less than its base. If the hypotenuse is 13 cm, find the other two sides.
solution:
Let the base = x cm, so the altitude = (x – 7) cm. Hypotenuse = 13 cm.
By the Pythagoras theorem: x² + (x–7)² = 13²
x² + x² – 14x + 49 = 169
2x² – 14x – 120 = 0
x² – 7x – 60 = 0
Factorising: (x – 12)(x + 5) = 0 → x = 12 or x = –5.
Since a side length cannot be negative, x = 12.
So the base = 12 cm and the altitude = 12 – 7 = 5 cm.
steps: Let base=x, altitude=x-7; apply Pythagoras theorem with hypotenuse 13
Solve x²-7x-60=0 by factorisation, reject negative root
Base = 12 cm, altitude = 5 cm

question: A cottage industry produces a certain number of pottery articles in a day. It was observed on a particular day that the cost of production of each article (in rupees) was 3 more than twice the number of articles produced on that day. If the total cost of production on that day was ₹90, find the number of articles produced and the cost of each article.
solution:
Let the number of articles produced = x. Cost of each article = (2x + 3) rupees.
Total cost: x(2x + 3) = 90 → 2x² + 3x – 90 = 0.
Discriminant = 3² + 4×2×90 = 9 + 720 = 729, √729 = 27.
x = (–3 ± 27)/4 = 24/4 = 6 or –30/4 (rejected, negative).
So x = 6.
Number of articles = 6, cost of each article = 2(6) + 3 = ₹15.
Check: 6 × 15 = 90 ✓
steps: Let articles=x, cost per article=2x+3; form 2x²+3x-90=0
Solve using the quadratic formula, discard the negative root

question: Find the nature of the roots of the following quadratic equations. If the real roots exist, find them: (i) 2x² – 3x + 5 = 0 (ii) 3x² – 4√3x + 4 = 0 (iii) 2x² – 6x + 3 = 0
solution:
(i) a=2, b=–3, c=5. Discriminant D = b² – 4ac = 9 – 40 = –31 < 0.
Since D < 0, the equation has no real roots.

(ii) a=3, b=–4√3, c=4. D = (4√3)² – 4×3×4 = 48 – 48 = 0.
Since D = 0, the equation has two equal real roots, given by x = –b/2a = 4√3/6 = 2√3/3 (both roots).

(iii) a=2, b=–6, c=3. D = 36 – 24 = 12 > 0.
Since D > 0, the equation has two distinct real roots:
x = [–b ± √D] / 2a = [6 ± √12]/4 = [6 ± 2√3]/4 = (3 ± √3)/2.
So x = (3+√3)/2 or x = (3–√3)/2.
steps: Compute the discriminant D = b²-4ac for each equation
D<0: no real roots; D=0: equal real roots; D>0: two distinct real roots
(i) no real roots (ii) equal roots 2√3/3 (iii) distinct roots (3±√3)/2

question: Find the values of k for each of the following quadratic equations, so that they have two equal roots: (i) 2x² + kx + 3 = 0 (ii) kx(x – 2) + 6 = 0
solution:
(i) a=2, b=k, c=3. For equal roots, discriminant = 0: k² – 4×2×3 = 0 → k² = 24 → k = ±√24 = ±2√6.

(ii) kx(x–2) + 6 = 0 → kx² – 2kx + 6 = 0. Here a=k, b=–2k, c=6 (k ≠ 0 for it to be quadratic).
Discriminant = 0: (–2k)² – 4×k×6 = 0 → 4k² – 24k = 0 → 4k(k – 6) = 0 → k = 0 or k = 6.
Since k = 0 makes the equation non-quadratic (linear), we reject it. So k = 6.
steps: Set discriminant b²-4ac = 0 for equal roots

question: Is it possible to design a rectangular mango grove whose length is twice its breadth, and the area is 800 m²? If so, find its length and breadth.
solution:
Let the breadth = x m, so the length = 2x m.
Area: 2x × x = 800 → 2x² = 800 → x² = 400 → x = ±20.
Since breadth cannot be negative, x = 20.
Discriminant of x² – 400 = 0 is positive (it factors directly), so real roots exist — yes, it is possible.
Breadth = 20 m, Length = 2 × 20 = 40 m.

question: Is the following situation possible? If so, determine their present ages. The sum of the ages of two friends is 20 years. Four years ago, the product of their ages in years was 48.
solution:
Let one friend's present age = x years, so the other's = (20 – x) years.
Four years ago: ages were (x – 4) and (16 – x).
Product: (x–4)(16–x) = 48 → 16x – x² – 64 + 4x = 48 → –x² + 20x – 64 = 48 → –x² + 20x – 112 = 0 → x² – 20x + 112 = 0.
Discriminant = 400 – 448 = –48 < 0.
Since the discriminant is negative, this quadratic equation has no real roots. Therefore, the given situation is not possible.

question: Is it possible to design a rectangular park of perimeter 80 m and area 400 m²? If so, find its length and breadth.
solution:
Let length = x m and breadth = y m.
Perimeter: 2(x+y) = 80 → x + y = 40 → y = 40 – x.
Area: xy = 400 → x(40–x) = 400 → 40x – x² = 400 → x² – 40x + 400 = 0.
Discriminant = 1600 – 1600 = 0.
Since D = 0, real (equal) roots exist, so it is possible.
x = –b/2a = 40/2 = 20. Then y = 40 – 20 = 20.
So the length and breadth are both 20 m — the park is a square (a special rectangle) of side 20 m.
steps: Let length=x, breadth=40-x (from perimeter); form x²-40x+400=0
Discriminant = 0, so equal roots exist: x=20
Yes, possible: a 20 m × 20 m square park

question: In which of the following situations, does the list of numbers involved make an arithmetic progression, and why? (ii) The amount of air present in a cylinder when a vacuum pump removes 1/4 of the air remaining in the cylinder at a time. (iii) The cost of digging a well after every metre of digging, when it costs ₹150 for the first metre and rises by ₹50 for each subsequent metre. (iv) The amount of money in the account every year, when ₹10000 is deposited at compound interest at 8% per annum.
solution:
(i) Fares are 15, 23, 31, 39, ... (each additional km adds ₹8). The difference between consecutive terms is always 8, a constant. So yes, it forms an AP.

(ii) If initial air = V, then after each removal the air remaining is V, (3/4)V, (3/4)²V, ... Each term is obtained by multiplying by 3/4, not adding a fixed number, so the differences are not constant. It does not form an AP.

(iii) Costs are 150, 200, 250, 300, ... with a constant difference of 50. So yes, it forms an AP.

(iv) Amounts are 10000, 10000(1.08), 10000(1.08)², ... — this grows multiplicatively (geometric), not by a fixed added amount. It does not form an AP.

question: How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 7?
solution:

question: For what value of n, are the nth terms of two APs: 63, 65, 67, ... and 3, 10, 17, ... equal?

63–3 = 7(n–1)–2(n–1)

question: If the sum of the first n terms of an AP is 4n – n², what is the first term (that is S₁)? What is the sum of first two terms? What is the second term? Similarly, find the 3rd, the 10th and the nth terms.
solution:

a₁₀ = a+9d = 3–18 = –15.
aₙ = a+(n–1)d = 3+(n–1)(–2) = 3–2n+2 = 5–2n.
steps: S₁ gives the first term directly; a₂ = S₂ - S₁

question: In a school, students thought of planting trees in and around the school to reduce air pollution. It was decided that the number of trees, that each section of each class will plant, will be the same as the class, in which they are studying, e.g., a section of Class I will plant 1 tree, a section of Class II will plant 2 trees and so on till Class XII. There are three sections of each class. How many trees will be planted by the students?
solution:
For each class k (k=1 to 12), each of the 3 sections plants k trees, so class k plants 3k trees in total.
Total trees = Σ(k=1 to 12) 3k = 3 × [12×13/2] = 3×78 = 234.
steps: Each class k contributes 3k trees (3 sections × k trees each)

Total trees planted = 234

question: A spiral is made up of successive semicircles, with centres alternately at A and B, starting with centre at A, of radii 0.5 cm, 1.0 cm, 1.5 cm, 2.0 cm, ... What is the total length of such a spiral made up of thirteen consecutive semicircles? (Take π = 22/7)
solution:
The length of a semicircle of radius r is πr. Since the radii are 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, ... (an AP with first term 0.5 and common difference 0.5), the semicircle lengths l₁, l₂, ... also form an AP with a = π×0.5 = 11/7 and d = π×0.5 = 11/7 (using π=22/7).
For n=13 semicircles:
S₁₃ = (13/2)[2a + 12d] = (13/2)[2×(11/7) + 12×(11/7)] = (13/2)×(14×11/7) = (13/2)×22 = 13×11 = 143.
The total length of the spiral is 143 cm.
steps: Semicircle length = πr; radii form an AP, so lengths form an AP too with a=d=π×0.5
Apply Sₙ = (n/2)[2a+(n-1)d] with n=13, π=22/7
Total length = 143 cm

question: 200 logs are stacked in the following manner: 20 logs in the bottom row, 19 in the next row, 18 in the row next to it and so on. In how many rows are the 200 logs placed and how many logs are in the top row?
solution:
a=20, d=–1, S=200.
Sₙ = (n/2)[40–(n–1)] = 200 → n(41–n) = 400 → 41n–n² = 400 → n²–41n+400 = 0.
Discriminant = 1681–1600 = 81 = 9². n = (41±9)/2 = 25 or 16.
Since the number of logs per row (aₙ = 21–n) must stay positive (n < 21), n = 16 is the valid answer (n=25 would require negative logs in later rows).
a₁₆ = 20 – 15 = 5.
So there are 16 rows, with 5 logs in the top row.
steps: Form the equation n²-41n+400=0 from Sₙ=200
Solve to get n=16 or n=25; reject n=25 as it gives negative log counts
16 rows, with 5 logs in the top row

question: In a potato race, a bucket is placed at the starting point, which is 5 m from the first potato, and the other potatoes are placed 3 m apart in a straight line. There are ten potatoes in the line. A competitor starts from the bucket, picks up the nearest potato, runs back with it, drops it in the bucket, runs back to pick up the next potato, runs to the bucket to drop it in, and continues in the same way until all the potatoes are in the bucket. What is the total distance the competitor has to run?
solution:
Distance to fetch and return the nth potato = 2×[5+3(n–1)] (there and back).
These distances form an AP with a=2×5=10, d=2×3=6, n=10.
Total distance = S₁₀ = (10/2)[2×10 + 9×6] = 5[20+54] = 5×74 = 370.
The competitor has to run a total distance of 370 m.
steps: Distance for nth potato round trip = 2×[5+3(n-1)], forming an AP with a=10, d=6
Apply Sₙ = (n/2)[2a+(n-1)d] for n=10
Total distance run = 370 m

question: Which term of the AP: 121, 117, 113, ..., is its first negative term?
solution:

The smallest integer n satisfying this is n=32.
a₃₂ = 121+31×(–4) = 121–124 = –3.
So the 32nd term, equal to –3, is the first negative term.
steps: Set aₙ < 0 and solve the inequality for n
n > 31.25, so smallest integer n = 32
The 32nd term (= –3) is the first negative term

question: The sum of the third and the seventh terms of an AP is 6 and their product is 8. Find the sum of first sixteen terms of the AP.
solution:
a₃+a₇ = 6 → (a+2d)+(a+6d) = 6 → a+4d = 3 → a = 3–4d.
a₃×a₇ = 8 → (a+2d)(a+6d) = 8.
Substituting a=3–4d: a+2d = 3–2d, a+6d = 3+2d. Product = (3–2d)(3+2d) = 9–4d² = 8 → 4d² = 1 → d = ±1/2.

Case d = 1/2: a = 3–2 = 1.
S₁₆ = (16/2)[2×1 + 15×(1/2)] = 8[2+7.5] = 8×9.5 = 76.

Case d = –1/2: a = 3+2 = 5.
S₁₆ = (16/2)[2×5 + 15×(–1/2)] = 8[10–7.5] = 8×2.5 = 20.

So the sum of the first sixteen terms is 76 or 20, depending on which AP (increasing or decreasing) is considered.
steps: Use a₃+a₇=6 to get a+4d=3, then a₃×a₇=8 to get 9-4d²=8, so d=±1/2
Find corresponding a for each value of d
S₁₆ = 76 (for d=1/2) or 20 (for d=-1/2)

question: A ladder has rungs 25 cm apart. The rungs decrease uniformly in length from 45 cm at the bottom to 25 cm at the top. If the top and the bottom rungs are 2½ m apart, what is the length of the wood required for the rungs?
solution:
Distance between top and bottom rungs = 2.5 m = 250 cm, and rungs are 25 cm apart, so the number of rungs = 250/25 + 1 = 11.
The rung lengths form an AP with a=45 (bottom), l=25 (top), n=11.
Total wood required = sum of all rung lengths = (n/2)(a+l) = (11/2)(45+25) = (11/2)×70 = 11×35 = 385.
The length of wood required for the rungs is 385 cm.
steps: Number of rungs = (total gap)/(spacing) + 1 = 250/25+1 = 11
Rung lengths form an AP from 45 cm to 25 cm
Total wood = (n/2)(a+l) = 385 cm

question: The houses of a row are numbered consecutively from 1 to 49. Show that there is a value of x such that the sum of the numbers of the houses preceding the house numbered x is equal to the sum of the numbers of the houses following it. Find this value of x.
solution:
Sum of house numbers before x (i.e., 1 to x–1) = (x–1)x/2.
Sum of house numbers after x (i.e., x+1 to 49) = [sum of 1 to 49] – [sum of 1 to x] = 49×50/2 – x(x+1)/2 = 1225 – x(x+1)/2.
Setting these equal:
(x–1)x/2 = 1225 – x(x+1)/2
Multiplying throughout by 2: x(x–1) = 2450 – x(x+1)
x² – x = 2450 – x² – x
2x² = 2450 → x² = 1225 → x = 35 (taking the positive value within the range 1–49).

Verification: Sum before 35 (1 to 34) = 34×35/2 = 595. Sum after 35 (36 to 49) = 1225 – (35×36/2) = 1225–630 = 595. Equal, confirming x=35.
steps: Write expressions for the sum before x and the sum after x using AP sum formulas
Set the two sums equal and simplify to x²=1225
x = 35 (verified: both sums equal 595)

question: A small terrace at a football ground comprises of 15 steps each of which is 50 m long and built of solid concrete. Each step has a rise of ¼ m and a tread of ½ m. Calculate the total volume of concrete required to build the terrace.
solution:
The volume of concrete in the nth step (counting from the top) equals length × tread × (cumulative rise up to that step) = 50 × (1/2) × (n × 1/4) = 50n/8 = 6.25n cubic metres.
This forms an AP with a = 6.25, d = 6.25 (since consecutive volumes differ by 6.25), n = 15.
Total volume = Σ(n=1 to 15) 6.25n = 6.25 × [15×16/2] = 6.25×120 = 750.
The total volume of concrete required is 750 m³.
steps: Volume for the nth step = 50 × (1/2) × (n/4) = 6.25n cubic metres, forming an AP
Sum this AP for n=1 to 15 (equivalently 6.25 × sum of first 15 natural numbers)
Total volume required = 750 m³

question:
Fill in the blanks using the correct word given in brackets:
(i) All circles are ______. (congruent, similar)
(ii) All squares are ______. (similar, congruent)
(iii) All ______ triangles are similar. (isosceles, equilateral)
(iv) Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (a) their corresponding angles are ______ and (b) their corresponding sides are ______. (equal, proportional)
solution:
(i) All circles are similar (any circle can be enlarged/reduced to match any other circle, so shape is always the same).
(ii) All squares are similar (all angles are 90° and all sides are in the same ratio 1:1).
(iii) All equilateral triangles are similar (all angles are 60° and all sides are in equal ratio).
(iv) (a) equal, (b) proportional — two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional.
steps: Similar figures have the same shape (equal angles, proportional sides), size may differ
A circle/square/equilateral triangle always has the same angles and side-ratios, so any two of them are similar
Similarity of polygons needs BOTH equal corresponding angles AND proportional corresponding sides

question: Give two different examples of pairs of (i) similar figures, (ii) non-similar figures.
solution:
(i) Similar figures: (a) Any two circles (of different radii) are similar, since they always have the same shape. (b) Any two squares (of different side lengths) are similar, since all angles are 90° and all sides are in the same ratio.
(ii) Non-similar figures: (a) A circle and a square are not similar (different shapes altogether). (b) A rectangle (non-square) and a square are not similar in general, since their sides are not in the same ratio even though all angles are 90°.
steps: Similar = same shape, i.e., equal angles and proportional sides (size can differ)
Any two circles, or any two squares, or any two equilateral triangles are always similar
Two figures with a different overall shape (e.g. circle vs square, or a general rectangle vs a square) are non-similar

question:
E and F are points on the sides PQ and PR respectively of a △PQR. For each of the following cases, state whether EF || QR:
(i) PE = 3.9 cm, EQ = 3 cm, PF = 3.6 cm and FR = 2.4 cm
(ii) PE = 4 cm, QE = 4.5 cm, PF = 8 cm and RF = 9 cm
(iii) PQ = 1.28 cm, PR = 2.56 cm, PE = 0.18 cm and PF = 0.36 cm
solution:
By the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales' theorem), EF || QR if and only if PE/EQ = PF/FR.
(i) PE/EQ = 3.9/3 = 1.3, and PF/FR = 3.6/2.4 = 1.5. Since 1.3 ≠ 1.5, EF is NOT parallel to QR.
(ii) PE/QE = 4/4.5 = 8/9, and PF/RF = 8/9. Since 8/9 = 8/9, EF IS parallel to QR.
(iii) EQ = PQ − PE = 1.28 − 0.18 = 1.10 cm, and FR = PR − PF = 2.56 − 0.36 = 2.20 cm.
PE/EQ = 0.18/1.10 = 9/55, and PF/FR = 0.36/2.20 = 9/55. Since these are equal, EF IS parallel to QR.
steps: Converse of BPT: if PE/EQ = PF/FR, then EF || QR
(ii) 4/4.5 = 8/8 = 9/9 → parallel; (iii) find EQ, FR by subtraction, ratios equal (9/55) → parallel

question: Using Theorem 6.1 (Basic Proportionality Theorem), prove that a line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side.
solution:
Let ABC be a triangle in which D is the mid-point of AB, and DE is drawn parallel to BC, meeting AC at E. We need to prove that E is the mid-point of AC.
Since DE || BC, by Theorem 6.1 (Basic Proportionality Theorem) applied to △ABC:
AD/DB = AE/EC
Since D is the mid-point of AB, AD = DB, so AD/DB = 1.
Therefore AE/EC = 1, which gives AE = EC.
Hence E is the mid-point of AC, i.e., the line DE parallel to BC bisects the third side AC.
steps: Draw DE || BC through midpoint D of AB, meeting AC at E
By BPT: AD/DB = AE/EC
AD = DB (D is midpoint) ⟹ AE = EC ⟹ E is midpoint of AC

question: Using Theorem 6.2 (converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem), prove that the line joining the mid-points of any two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side.
solution:
Let ABC be a triangle in which D and E are the mid-points of sides AB and AC respectively. We need to prove DE || BC.
Since D is the mid-point of AB, AD = DB, so AD/DB = 1.
Since E is the mid-point of AC, AE = EC, so AE/EC = 1.
Therefore AD/DB = AE/EC (both equal to 1).
By Theorem 6.2 (converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem), since AD/DB = AE/EC, we conclude DE || BC.
Hence the line joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side.
steps: D, E are midpoints of AB, AC ⟹ AD/DB = 1 and AE/EC = 1
So AD/DB = AE/EC
By converse of BPT (Theorem 6.2), DE || BC

question: ABCD is a trapezium in which AB || DC and its diagonals intersect each other at the point O. Show that AO/BO = CO/DO.
solution:
In △OAB and △OCD:
∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite angles)
∠OAB = ∠OCD (alternate angles, since AB || DC and AC is a transversal)
Therefore, by AA similarity criterion, △OAB ~ △OCD.
Since corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional:
OA/OC = OB/OD
which can be rewritten as OA/OB = OC/OD.
Hence AO/BO = CO/DO, as required.
steps: AB || DC ⟹ ∠OAB=∠OCD and ∠OBA=∠ODC (alternate angles)
By AA, △OAB ~ △OCD
Corresponding sides proportional: OA/OC = OB/OD ⟹ AO/BO = CO/DO

question: The diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD intersect each other at the point O such that AO/BO = CO/DO. Show that ABCD is a trapezium.
solution:
Given: AO/BO = CO/DO, i.e., AO·DO = BO·CO ... (*)
Draw a line EO through O parallel to AB, meeting AD at E.
In △DAB, since EO || AB, by the Basic Proportionality Theorem: DE/EA = DO/OB ... (1)
From the given condition, AO/BO = CO/DO ⟹ AO/CO = BO/DO, i.e., BO/DO = AO/CO, which gives DO/OB = CO/AO, i.e., AE/ED (taking reciprocal of (1)) needs to be compared:
From (1), EA/ED = OB/DO. From the given ratio, OB/DO = AO/CO. So EA/ED = AO/CO, i.e., AE/ED = AO/OC.
Now consider △ACD: since AE/ED = AO/OC, by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Theorem 6.2) applied to △ACD, EO || DC.
But EO || AB (by construction). Since EO is parallel to both AB and DC, we conclude AB || DC.
Hence ABCD is a trapezium (with AB || DC).
steps: Draw EO || AB through O, meeting AD at E
In △DAB, BPT gives DE/EA = DO/OB
Given ratio AO/BO=CO/DO rearranges to show AE/ED = AO/OC; converse BPT in △ACD gives EO || DC
EO || AB and EO || DC ⟹ AB || DC ⟹ ABCD is a trapezium

question: In the given figure, △ODC ~ △OBA, ∠BOC = 125° and ∠CDO = 70°. Find ∠DOC, ∠DCO and ∠OAB.
solution:
Since O lies on both diagonals, B, O, D are collinear, so ∠BOC and ∠DOC form a linear pair:
∠DOC = 180° − ∠BOC = 180° − 125° = 55°
In △ODC, using the angle sum property:
∠ODC + ∠OCD + ∠DOC = 180°
70° + ∠OCD + 55° = 180°
∠OCD = 180° − 125° = 55°, so ∠DCO = 55°
Since △ODC ~ △OBA, corresponding angles are equal: ∠OCD (at C) corresponds to ∠OAB (at A).
Therefore ∠OAB = ∠OCD = 55°.
steps: ∠BOC and ∠DOC are supplementary (B,O,D collinear) ⟹ ∠DOC = 55°
Angle sum in △ODC: ∠DCO = 180−70−55 = 55°
△ODC~△OBA ⟹ ∠OCD corresponds to ∠OAB ⟹ ∠OAB = 55°

question: Diagonals AC and BD of a trapezium ABCD with AB || DC intersect each other at the point O. Using a similarity criterion for two triangles, show that OA/OC = OB/OD.
solution:
In △OAB and △OCD:
∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite angles)
∠OAB = ∠OCD (alternate angles, since AB || DC and AC is a transversal)
Therefore, by the AA similarity criterion, △OAB ~ △OCD.
Since corresponding sides of similar triangles are in proportion:
OA/OC = OB/OD = AB/DC
Hence OA/OC = OB/OD, as required.
steps: AB || DC gives a pair of alternate angles equal, plus vertically opposite angles at O
By AA similarity criterion, △OAB ~ △OCD
Corresponding sides proportional: OA/OC = OB/OD

question: S and T are points on sides PR and QR of △PQR such that ∠P = ∠RTS. Show that △RPQ ~ △RTS.
solution:
In △RPQ and △RTS:
∠R is common to both triangles (∠PRQ = ∠TRS, same angle, since S lies on PR and T lies on QR)
∠RPQ = ∠RTS (given, ∠P = ∠RTS)
Therefore, by the AA similarity criterion, △RPQ ~ △RTS.
steps: ∠R is common to both triangles (S on PR, T on QR)
∠RPQ = ∠RTS is given
By AA similarity criterion, △RPQ ~ △RTS

question: In the given figure, if △ABE ≅ △ACD, show that △ADE ~ △ABC.
solution:
Since △ABE ≅ △ACD, corresponding sides of congruent triangles are equal:
AB = AC ... (1)
AE = AD ... (2)
From (1) and (2), since AD = AE and AB = AC, we get:
AD/AB = AE/AC
(both ratios are equal because the numerators are equal to each other and the denominators are equal to each other)
Also, ∠DAE = ∠BAC (the same angle at vertex A, since D lies on AC and E lies on AB).
Therefore, by the SAS similarity criterion (AD/AB = AE/AC and the included angle A common), △ADE ~ △ABC.
steps: △ABE ≅ △ACD ⟹ AB = AC and AE = AD (CPCT)
This gives AD/AB = AE/AC, and ∠A is common to both triangles
By SAS similarity criterion, △ADE ~ △ABC

question:
In the given figure, altitudes AD and CE of △ABC intersect each other at the point P. Show that:
(i) △AEP ~ △CDP
(ii) △ABD ~ △CBE
(iii) △AEP ~ △ADB
(iv) △PDC ~ △BEC
solution:
(i) In △AEP and △CDP: ∠AEP = 90° (since CE ⊥ AB) and ∠CDP = 90° (since AD ⊥ BC), so ∠AEP = ∠CDP. Also ∠APE = ∠CPD (vertically opposite angles, as A,P,D and C,P,E are collinear pairs). By AA similarity, △AEP ~ △CDP.
(ii) In △ABD and △CBE: ∠ADB = 90° (AD ⊥ BC) and ∠CEB = 90° (CE ⊥ AB), so ∠ADB = ∠CEB. Also ∠ABD = ∠CBE (common angle B). By AA similarity, △ABD ~ △CBE.
(iii) In △AEP and △ADB: ∠AEP = 90° = ∠ADB. Also ∠EAP = ∠DAB (the same angle at A, since P lies on AD and E lies on AB). By AA similarity, △AEP ~ △ADB.
(iv) In △PDC and △BEC: ∠PDC = 90° (AD ⊥ BC) and ∠BEC = 90° (CE ⊥ AB), so ∠PDC = ∠BEC. Also ∠PCD = ∠BCE (common angle C, since P lies on CE and D lies on BC). By AA similarity, △PDC ~ △BEC.
steps: Right angles from the two altitudes (AD⊥BC, CE⊥AB) give a 90° pair in each case
(i) uses vertically opposite angles at P; (ii),(iii),(iv) use a common angle (B, A, C respectively)
Each pair is proved similar by the AA similarity criterion

question: E is a point on the side AD produced of a parallelogram ABCD and BE intersects CD at F. Show that △ABE ~ △CFB.
solution:
Since ABCD is a parallelogram, AB || DC and AD || BC.
E lies on AD produced, so AE is along the same line as AD, hence AE || BC.
Since AE || BC and BE (i.e., line BEF) is a transversal cutting them: ∠AEB = ∠FBC (alternate interior angles) ... (1)
Also, AB || DC, and the same transversal (line BEF, meeting DC at F) cuts them: ∠ABE = ∠CFB (alternate interior angles) ... (2)
From (1) and (2), two pairs of corresponding angles are equal, so by the AA similarity criterion, △ABE ~ △CFB.
steps: ABCD parallelogram ⟹ AD||BC and AB||DC
E on AD produced ⟹ AE||BC; transversal BEF gives ∠AEB = ∠FBC (alternate angles)
AB||DC with same transversal gives ∠ABE = ∠CFB; by AA, △ABE ~ △CFB

question:
In the given figure, ABC and AMP are two right triangles, right angled at B and M respectively. Prove that:
(i) △ABC ~ △AMP
(ii) CA/PA = BC/MP
solution:
(i) In △ABC and △AMP:
∠ABC = ∠AMP = 90° (given, right angles at B and M)
∠A is common to both triangles (the same angle at the common vertex A)
Therefore, by the AA similarity criterion, △ABC ~ △AMP.
(ii) Since △ABC ~ △AMP, corresponding sides are proportional:
CA/PA = BC/MP = AB/AM
Hence CA/PA = BC/MP, as required.
steps: ∠B = ∠M = 90° and ∠A is common to both right triangles
By AA similarity criterion, △ABC ~ △AMP
Corresponding sides proportional: CA/PA = BC/MP

question:
CD and GH are respectively the bisectors of ∠ACB and ∠EGF such that D and H lie on sides AB and FE of △ABC and △EFG respectively. If △ABC ~ △FEG, show that:
(i) CD/GH = AC/FG
(ii) △DCB ~ △HGE
(iii) △DCA ~ △HGF
solution:
Since △ABC ~ △FEG: ∠A = ∠F, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠G ... (1)
Since CD bisects ∠ACB and GH bisects ∠EGF (=∠FGE), and ∠C = ∠G:
∠ACD = ∠BCD = ∠C/2 and ∠FGH = ∠EGH = ∠G/2, so ∠ACD = ∠FGH and ∠BCD = ∠EGH ... (2)
(iii) In △DCA and △HGF: ∠A = ∠F (from (1)) and ∠ACD = ∠FGH (from (2)). By AA similarity, △DCA ~ △HGF.
(i) From the similarity in (iii), corresponding sides are proportional: CD/GH = CA/GF = DA/HF. Hence CD/GH = AC/FG.
(ii) In △DCB and △HGE: ∠B = ∠E (from (1)) and ∠BCD = ∠EGH (from (2)). By AA similarity, △DCB ~ △HGE.
steps: △ABC~△FEG gives ∠A=∠F, ∠B=∠E, ∠C=∠G; bisected angles give ∠ACD=∠FGH and ∠BCD=∠EGH
(iii) AA similarity: △DCA ~ △HGF using ∠A=∠F, ∠ACD=∠FGH
(i) follows from (iii)'s side ratio CD/GH=CA/GF; (ii) AA similarity △DCB ~ △HGE using ∠B=∠E, ∠BCD=∠EGH

question: In the given figure, E is a point on side CB produced of an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC. If AD ⊥ BC and EF ⊥ AC, prove that △ABD ~ △ECF.
solution:
Since E lies on CB produced, C, B, E are collinear, so ray CE is the same as ray CB, and F lies on line AC, so ray CF is the same as ray CA. Hence ∠ECF = ∠BCA (same angle).
Since AB = AC (given, isosceles triangle), the base angles are equal: ∠ABC = ∠ACB.
Now, ∠ABD = ∠ABC (since D lies on BC) = ∠ACB = ∠ECF (shown above). So ∠ABD = ∠ECF ... (1)
Also, ∠ADB = 90° (since AD ⊥ BC) and ∠EFC = 90° (since EF ⊥ AC), so ∠ADB = ∠EFC ... (2)
From (1) and (2), by the AA similarity criterion, △ABD ~ △ECF.
steps: AB = AC ⟹ ∠ABC = ∠ACB (base angles of isosceles triangle)
E on CB produced ⟹ ∠ECF = ∠ACB = ∠ABC = ∠ABD
AD⊥BC and EF⊥AC give ∠ADB = ∠EFC = 90°; by AA, △ABD ~ △ECF

question: Sides AB and BC and median AD of a triangle ABC are respectively proportional to sides PQ and QR and median PM of △PQR. Show that △ABC ~ △PQR.
solution:
Given: AB/PQ = BC/QR = AD/PM
Since AD and PM are medians, D is the mid-point of BC and M is the mid-point of QR, so BD = BC/2 and QM = QR/2.
Therefore, BD/QM = BC/QR = AB/PQ (dividing BC and QR by 2 does not change the ratio).
So in △ABD and △PQM: AB/PQ = BD/QM = AD/PM (all three pairs of corresponding sides proportional).
By the SSS similarity criterion, △ABD ~ △PQM.
Therefore, corresponding angles are equal: ∠ABD = ∠PQM, i.e., ∠ABC = ∠PQR (since D lies on BC and M lies on QR, these are the same angles).
Now, in △ABC and △PQR: AB/PQ = BC/QR (given) and the included angle ∠ABC = ∠PQR (just proved).
By the SAS similarity criterion, △ABC ~ △PQR.
steps: D, M are midpoints (medians) ⟹ BD/QM = BC/QR = AB/PQ = AD/PM
By SSS similarity, △ABD ~ △PQM ⟹ ∠ABD = ∠PQM, i.e. ∠ABC = ∠PQR
In △ABC, △PQR: AB/PQ = BC/QR with included angle B = Q equal ⟹ SAS similarity gives △ABC ~ △PQR

question: D is a point on the side BC of a triangle ABC such that ∠ADC = ∠BAC. Show that CA² = CB·CD.
solution:
In △CDA and △CAB (i.e., considering the angles at C, D/A, A/B):
∠ACD = ∠BCA (common angle C, same angle since D lies on BC)
∠ADC = ∠BAC (given)
Therefore, by the AA similarity criterion, △CDA ~ △CAB (with correspondence C↔C, D↔A, A↔B).
Since corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional:
CD/CA = CA/CB
Cross-multiplying: CA² = CB · CD, as required.
steps: ∠ACD = ∠BCA (common angle C) and ∠ADC = ∠BAC (given)
By AA similarity, △CDA ~ △CAB
Corresponding sides: CD/CA = CA/CB ⟹ CA² = CB·CD

question: Sides AB and AC and median AD of a triangle ABC are respectively proportional to sides PQ and PR and median PM of another triangle PQR. Show that △ABC ~ △PQR.
solution:
Given: AB/PQ = AC/PR = AD/PM.
Produce AD to E such that AD = DE, and produce PM to N such that PM = MN. Join CE and RN.
Since D is the mid-point of BC and also of AE, the diagonals of quadrilateral ABEC bisect each other, so ABEC is a parallelogram. Hence CE = AB (opposite sides of a parallelogram) ... (1)
Similarly, PQNR is a parallelogram, so RN = PQ ... (2)
Also, since AD = DE and PM = MN, AE = 2AD and PN = 2PM, so AE/PN = AD/PM ... (3)
From the given ratios and (1), (2), (3):
AC/PR = AB/PQ = CE/RN = AE/PN
So in △ACE and △PRN, all three pairs of sides are proportional (AC/PR = CE/RN = AE/PN). By the SSS similarity criterion, △ACE ~ △PRN, giving ∠CAE = ∠RPN, i.e. ∠CAD = ∠RPM (since E lies on AD produced and N on PM produced) ... (I)
By a similar argument, comparing △ABE and △PQN using AB/PQ = BE/QN (as BE = AC from the parallelogram) = AE/PN, we get △ABE ~ △PQN (SSS), giving ∠BAE = ∠QPN, i.e. ∠BAD = ∠QPM ... (II)
Adding (I) and (II): ∠BAD + ∠DAC = ∠QPM + ∠MPR, i.e. ∠BAC = ∠QPR.
Now in △ABC and △PQR: AB/PQ = AC/PR (given) and the included angle ∠BAC = ∠QPR (just shown). By the SAS similarity criterion, △ABC ~ △PQR.
steps: Extend medians AD, PM to E, N with AD=DE, PM=MN, forming parallelograms ABEC, PQNR
This gives CE=AB, RN=PQ, and AE/PN = AD/PM = given ratio; SSS similarity gives △ACE~△PRN and △ABE~△PQN
These give ∠CAD=∠RPM and ∠BAD=∠QPM; adding gives ∠BAC=∠QPR
SAS similarity in △ABC, △PQR (AB/PQ=AC/PR, included angle A=P) gives △ABC ~ △PQR

question: A vertical pole of length 6 m casts a shadow 4 m long on the ground and at the same time a tower casts a shadow 28 m long. Find the height of the tower.
solution:
At the same time of day, the sun's rays make the same angle with the ground everywhere, so the pole and its shadow, and the tower and its shadow, form similar right triangles (equal corresponding angles).
Therefore: (height of pole)/(length of pole's shadow) = (height of tower)/(length of tower's shadow)
6/4 = h/28
h = (6 × 28)/4 = 168/4 = 42
Hence the height of the tower is 42 m.
steps: Pole and tower with their shadows form similar right triangles (same sun angle)
height/shadow ratio is the same: 6/4 = h/28

question: If AD and PM are medians of triangles ABC and PQR respectively, where △ABC ~ △PQR, prove that AB/PQ = AD/PM.
solution:
Since △ABC ~ △PQR: AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP, and ∠B = ∠Q ... (1)
Since AD and PM are medians, D and M are mid-points of BC and QR respectively, so BD = BC/2 and QM = QR/2.
Therefore BD/QM = BC/QR = AB/PQ (from (1)) ... (2)
Also ∠ABD = ∠PQM (since D lies on BC, M lies on QR, these angles are the same as ∠B and ∠Q which are equal from (1)) ... (3)
In △ABD and △PQM: AB/PQ = BD/QM (from (2)) and the included angle ∠ABD = ∠PQM (from (3)).
By the SAS similarity criterion, △ABD ~ △PQM.
Therefore, corresponding sides are proportional: AB/PQ = AD/PM, as required.
steps: △ABC~△PQR gives AB/PQ=BC/QR and ∠B=∠Q
D, M are midpoints ⟹ BD/QM = BC/QR = AB/PQ, and ∠ABD=∠PQM
SAS similarity: △ABD ~ △PQM ⟹ AB/PQ = AD/PM

question:
Find the distance between the following pairs of points:
(i) (2, 3), (4, 1)
(ii) (–5, 7), (–1, 3)
(iii) (a, b), (–a, –b)
solution:
Using the distance formula, distance = √[(x₂–x₁)² + (y₂–y₁)²]
(i) (2,3) and (4,1): d = √[(4–2)² + (1–3)²] = √[4+4] = √8 = 2√2 units
(ii) (–5,7) and (–1,3): d = √[(–1+5)² + (3–7)²] = √[16+16] = √32 = 4√2 units
(iii) (a,b) and (–a,–b): d = √[(–a–a)² + (–b–b)²] = √[4a²+4b²] = 2√(a²+b²) units
steps: Distance formula: d = √[(x₂–x₁)² + (y₂–y₁)²]
(iii) √(4a²+4b²) = 2√(a²+b²)

question: Find the distance between the points (0, 0) and (36, 15). Can you now find the distance between the two towns A and B discussed in Section 7.2?
solution:
Distance = √[(36–0)² + (15–0)²] = √[1296 + 225] = √1521 = 39
So the distance between (0,0) and (36,15) is 39 units.
Since town A was taken as the origin (0,0) and town B as (36,15) with 1 km as one unit, the distance between towns A and B is also 39 km.
steps: Distance formula from origin: d = √(x²+y²)
So distance between towns A and B = 39 km

question: Determine if the points (1, 5), (2, 3) and (–2, –11) are collinear.
solution:
Let A(1,5), B(2,3), C(–2,–11).
AB = √[(2–1)² + (3–5)²] = √[1+4] = √5
BC = √[(–2–2)² + (–11–3)²] = √[16+196] = √212 = 2√53
AC = √[(–2–1)² + (–11–5)²] = √[9+256] = √265
For the points to be collinear, the sum of the two shorter distances must equal the longest one. Here AB + AC = √5 + √265 ≈ 2.24 + 16.28 = 18.5, which is not equal to BC ≈ 14.56; and no other combination of two distances adds up to the third either. Since AB + BC ≠ AC, AB + AC ≠ BC, and AC + BC ≠ AB, the three points are NOT collinear.
steps: Compute pairwise distances AB, BC, AC using the distance formula
No combination satisfies (sum of two) = (third), so the points are not collinear

question: Check whether (5, –2), (6, 4) and (7, –2) are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.
solution:
Let A(5,–2), B(6,4), C(7,–2).
AB = √[(6–5)² + (4+2)²] = √[1+36] = √37
BC = √[(7–6)² + (–2–4)²] = √[1+36] = √37
CA = √[(5–7)² + (–2+2)²] = √[4+0] = 2
Since AB = BC = √37, two sides are equal.
Hence (5,–2), (6,4) and (7,–2) are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.
steps: Compute the three side lengths using the distance formula
AB = BC, so the triangle is isosceles

question:
Name the type of quadrilateral formed, if any, by the following points, and give reasons for your answer:
(i) (–1, –2), (1, 0), (–1, 2), (–3, 0)
(ii) (–3, 5), (3, 1), (0, 3), (–1, –4)
(iii) (4, 5), (7, 6), (4, 3), (1, 2)
solution:
(i) Let A(–1,–2), B(1,0), C(–1,2), D(–3,0).
AB = √[(1+1)²+(0+2)²] = √8 = 2√2; BC = √[(–1–1)²+(2–0)²] = √8 = 2√2; CD = √[(–3+1)²+(0–2)²] = √8 = 2√2; DA = √[(–1+3)²+(–2–0)²] = √8 = 2√2. All four sides are equal.
Diagonals: AC = √[(–1+1)²+(2+2)²] = √16 = 4; BD = √[(–3–1)²+(0–0)²] = √16 = 4. Diagonals are also equal.
Since all sides are equal and the diagonals are equal, ABCD is a SQUARE.

(ii) Let A(–3,5), B(3,1), C(0,3), D(–1,–4).
Slope of AB = (1–5)/(3+3) = –4/6 = –2/3. Slope of BC = (3–1)/(0–3) = 2/(–3) = –2/3.
Since slope of AB = slope of BC, the points A, B, C are collinear. So no quadrilateral can be formed with these four points — they do not form a proper quadrilateral.

(iii) Let A(4,5), B(7,6), C(4,3), D(1,2).
AB = √[(7–4)²+(6–5)²] = √10; BC = √[(4–7)²+(3–6)²] = √18 = 3√2; CD = √[(1–4)²+(2–3)²] = √10; DA = √[(4–1)²+(5–2)²] = √18 = 3√2.
Opposite sides are equal: AB = CD and BC = DA.
Diagonals: AC = √[(4–4)²+(3–5)²] = √4 = 2; BD = √[(1–7)²+(2–6)²] = √52 = 2√13. Diagonals are unequal.
Since opposite sides are equal but the diagonals are not equal, ABCD is a PARALLELOGRAM (but not a rectangle).
steps: (i) All 4 sides equal AND diagonals equal ⟹ square
(ii) Slope of AB = slope of BC ⟹ A, B, C collinear ⟹ no quadrilateral is formed
(iii) Opposite sides equal, diagonals unequal ⟹ parallelogram

question: Find the point on the x-axis which is equidistant from (2, –5) and (–2, 9).
solution:
Let the required point on the x-axis be P(x, 0).
Since P is equidistant from A(2,–5) and B(–2,9): PA² = PB²
(x–2)² + (0+5)² = (x+2)² + (0–9)²
x² – 4x + 4 + 25 = x² + 4x + 4 + 81
–4x + 29 = 4x + 85
–8x = 56
x = –7
So the required point is (–7, 0).
steps: Let point be (x,0) on x-axis; set PA² = PB²
Solve: –8x = 56 ⟹ x = –7; point is (–7,0)

question: Find the values of y for which the distance between the points P(2, –3) and Q(10, y) is 10 units.
steps: Set PQ² = 10² using distance formula

question: If Q(0, 1) is equidistant from P(5, –3) and R(x, 6), find the values of x. Also find the distances QR and PR.
solution:
Since Q is equidistant from P and R: QP² = QR²
QP² = (5–0)² + (–3–1)² = 25 + 16 = 41
QR² = (x–0)² + (6–1)² = x² + 25
Setting these equal: x² + 25 = 41 ⟹ x² = 16 ⟹ x = ±4
QR = √41 units (since QR² = 41, matching QP²).
For PR: if x = 4, PR = √[(5–4)²+(–3–6)²] = √[1+81] = √82 units.
If x = –4, PR = √[(5+4)²+(–3–6)²] = √[81+81] = √162 = 9√2 units.
So x = 4 or x = –4; QR = √41 units; and PR = √82 units (for x=4) or 9√2 units (for x=–4).
steps: Q equidistant from P, R ⟹ QP² = QR²
PR computed separately for x=4 (√82) and x=–4 (9√2)

question: Find a relation between x and y such that the point (x, y) is equidistant from the points (3, 6) and (–3, 4).
solution:
Let the point be P(x,y), A(3,6), B(–3,4). Given PA = PB, so PA² = PB².
(x–3)² + (y–6)² = (x+3)² + (y–4)²
x² – 6x + 9 + y² – 12y + 36 = x² + 6x + 9 + y² – 8y + 16
–6x – 12y + 45 = 6x – 8y + 25
–12x – 4y + 20 = 0
Dividing by –4: 3x + y – 5 = 0
So the required relation is 3x + y – 5 = 0 (i.e., 3x + y = 5).
steps: Set PA² = PB² for point (x,y) equidistant from (3,6) and (–3,4)
Expand and simplify both sides
Result: 3x + y – 5 = 0

question: Find the coordinates of the point which divides the join of (–1, 7) and (4, –3) in the ratio 2 : 3.
solution:
Using the section formula, for a point dividing (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) internally in ratio m₁:m₂:
x = (m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁+m₂), y = (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁+m₂)
Here (x₁,y₁)=(–1,7), (x₂,y₂)=(4,–3), m₁:m₂ = 2:3
x = [2(4) + 3(–1)]/(2+3) = (8–3)/5 = 1
y = [2(–3) + 3(7)]/(2+3) = (–6+21)/5 = 3
So the required point is (1, 3).
steps: Apply section formula with m₁:m₂ = 2:3

question: Find the coordinates of the points of trisection of the line segment joining (4, –1) and (–2, –3).
solution:
The two points of trisection P and Q divide the segment into three equal parts, so P divides it in ratio 1:2 and Q divides it in ratio 2:1 (both from (4,–1) towards (–2,–3)).
For P (ratio 1:2): x = [1(–2)+2(4)]/3 = (–2+8)/3 = 2; y = [1(–3)+2(–1)]/3 = (–3–2)/3 = –5/3
P = (2, –5/3)
For Q (ratio 2:1): x = [2(–2)+1(4)]/3 = (–4+4)/3 = 0; y = [2(–3)+1(–1)]/3 = (–6–1)/3 = –7/3
Q = (0, –7/3)
So the points of trisection are (2, –5/3) and (0, –7/3).
steps: Trisection points divide the segment in ratios 1:2 and 2:1
Apply section formula for ratio 1:2 → P = (2, –5/3)
Apply section formula for ratio 2:1 → Q = (0, –7/3)

question: To conduct Sports Day activities, in your rectangular shaped school ground ABCD, lines have been drawn with chalk powder at a distance of 1 m each. 100 flower pots have been placed at a distance of 1 m from each other along AD. Niharika runs 1/4th the distance AD on the 2nd line and posts a green flag. Preet runs 1/5th the distance AD on the eighth line and posts a red flag. What is the distance between both the flags? If Rashmi has to post a blue flag exactly halfway between the line segment joining the two flags, where should she post her flag?
solution:
Take A as the origin, with AB along the x-axis and AD along the y-axis. Since 100 flower pots are placed 1 m apart along AD, AD = 100 m, and the parallel lines are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... along AB (1 m apart), so the 2nd line is x = 2 and the 8th line is x = 8.
Niharika's green flag: on the 2nd line, at 1/4 of AD = 1/4 × 100 = 25 m, so position = (2, 25).
Preet's red flag: on the 8th line, at 1/5 of AD = 1/5 × 100 = 20 m, so position = (8, 20).
Distance between the flags = √[(8–2)² + (20–25)²] = √[36+25] = √61 m.

question: Find the ratio in which the line segment joining the points (–3, 10) and (6, –8) is divided by (–1, 6).
solution:
Let the point (–1,6) divide the segment joining A(–3,10) and B(6,–8) in the ratio k:1.
Using the section formula for the x-coordinate:
–1 = [k(6) + 1(–3)]/(k+1)
–1(k+1) = 6k – 3
–k – 1 = 6k – 3
2 = 7k
k = 2/7
So the ratio is k:1 = 2/7 : 1 = 2 : 7.
(Check with y-coordinate: y = [2(–8)+7(10)]/9 = (–16+70)/9 = 54/9 = 6 ✓, matches the given point.)
steps: Let ratio be k:1; use section formula on x-coordinate
Ratio = 2:7 (verified using y-coordinate)

question: Find the ratio in which the line segment joining A(1, –5) and B(–4, 5) is divided by the x-axis. Also find the coordinates of the point of division.
solution:
Let the x-axis divide AB in the ratio k:1 at the point where y = 0.
y-coordinate: 0 = [k(5) + 1(–5)]/(k+1)
0 = 5k – 5
k = 1
So the ratio is 1:1.
x-coordinate: x = [k(–4) + 1(1)]/(k+1) = [1(–4)+1]/(1+1) = –3/2
So the x-axis divides AB in the ratio 1:1, and the point of division is (–3/2, 0).
steps: Let ratio be k:1; set y-coordinate = 0 (point is on x-axis)
5k – 5 = 0 ⟹ k = 1, so ratio is 1:1

question: If (1, 2), (4, y), (x, 6) and (3, 5) are the vertices of a parallelogram taken in order, find x and y.
solution:
In a parallelogram, the diagonals bisect each other. Here the diagonals join (1,2)-(x,6) and (4,y)-(3,5).
Midpoint of (1,2) and (x,6) = midpoint of (4,y) and (3,5)
((1+x)/2, (2+6)/2) = ((4+3)/2, (y+5)/2)
From x-coordinates: (1+x)/2 = 7/2 ⟹ 1+x = 7 ⟹ x = 6
From y-coordinates: (2+6)/2 = (y+5)/2 ⟹ 8 = y+5 ⟹ y = 3
So x = 6 and y = 3.
steps: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
Set midpoint of (1,2)-(x,6) equal to midpoint of (4,y)-(3,5)
Solve: x = 6, y = 3

question: Find the coordinates of a point A, where AB is the diameter of a circle whose centre is (2, –3) and B is (1, 4).
solution:
Since AB is a diameter, the centre is the midpoint of A and B.
Let A = (x, y). Then:
(x+1)/2 = 2 ⟹ x+1 = 4 ⟹ x = 3
(y+4)/2 = –3 ⟹ y+4 = –6 ⟹ y = –10
So A = (3, –10).
steps: Centre is the midpoint of the diameter's endpoints A and B

question: Find the coordinates of the points which divide the line segment joining A(–2, 2) and B(2, 8) into four equal parts.
solution:
Let P₁, P₂, P₃ be the points dividing AB into four equal parts, so P₁ is at 1/4, P₂ (the midpoint) at 2/4, and P₃ at 3/4 of the way from A to B.
P₁ (ratio 1:3): x = [1(2)+3(–2)]/4 = (2–6)/4 = –1; y = [1(8)+3(2)]/4 = (8+6)/4 = 3.5 → P₁ = (–1, 3.5)
P₂ (midpoint, ratio 1:1): x = (–2+2)/2 = 0; y = (2+8)/2 = 5 → P₂ = (0, 5)
P₃ (ratio 3:1): x = [3(2)+1(–2)]/4 = (6–2)/4 = 1; y = [3(8)+1(2)]/4 = (24+2)/4 = 6.5 → P₃ = (1, 6.5)
So the three points dividing AB into four equal parts are (–1, 3.5), (0, 5) and (1, 6.5).
steps: Points divide AB in ratios 1:3, 1:1 (midpoint), and 3:1
Apply section formula for each ratio

question: Find the area of a rhombus if its vertices are (3, 0), (4, 5), (–1, 4) and (–2, –1) taken in order. [Hint: Area of a rhombus = (1/2)(product of its diagonals)]
solution:
The diagonals of the rhombus join opposite vertices: (3,0)-(–1,4) and (4,5)-(–2,–1).
Diagonal 1: d₁ = √[(–1–3)² + (4–0)²] = √[16+16] = √32 = 4√2
Diagonal 2: d₂ = √[(–2–4)² + (–1–5)²] = √[36+36] = √72 = 6√2
Area of rhombus = (1/2) × d₁ × d₂ = (1/2) × 4√2 × 6√2 = (1/2) × 48 = 24
So the area of the rhombus is 24 square units.
steps: Diagonals join opposite vertices (3,0)-(–1,4) and (4,5)-(–2,–1)
Area = (1/2)×d₁×d₂ = 24 sq units

question:
In △ABC, right-angled at B, AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm. Determine:
(i) sin A, cos A
(ii) sin C, cos C
solution:
Since △ABC is right-angled at B, by the Pythagoras theorem:

AC = 25 cm

cos A = (side adjacent to A)/hypotenuse = AB/AC = 24/25
(ii) sin C = (side opposite C)/hypotenuse = AB/AC = 24/25
cos C = (side adjacent to C)/hypotenuse = BC/AC = 7/25

sin C = AB/AC = 24/25, cos C = BC/AC = 7/25

question: If sin A = 3/4, calculate cos A and tan A.
solution:

cos A = √7/4
tan A = sin A/cos A = (3/4)/(√7/4) = 3/√7

question: Given 15 cot A = 8, find sin A and sec A.
solution:

Consider a right triangle with side opposite A = 15, side adjacent to A = 8. Then hypotenuse = √(15² + 8²) = √(225+64) = √289 = 17.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = 15/17
sec A = hypotenuse/adjacent = 17/8

Hypotenuse = √(15²+8²) = 17

question: Given sec θ = 13/12, calculate all other trigonometric ratios.

question: If ∠A and ∠B are acute angles such that cos A = cos B, then show that ∠A = ∠B.
solution:
Consider two right triangles with the same hypotenuse h: one containing angle A, the other angle B, such that cos A = cos B = k.
In each triangle, the side adjacent to the angle = hypotenuse × cos(angle) = h·k. Since this is the same value (h·k) in both triangles, the adjacent sides of the two right triangles are equal.
By the Pythagoras theorem, the side opposite the angle = √(h² – (hk)²), which is also the same in both triangles (since h and k are the same).
So the two right triangles have all three corresponding sides equal — they are congruent (by the RHS/SSS criterion).
Since the triangles are congruent, their corresponding angles are equal, so ∠A = ∠B.
steps: Consider two right triangles with the same hypotenuse h, where cos A = cos B = k
Adjacent side = hk (same in both); opposite side = √(h²–h²k²) (same in both, by Pythagoras)
All three sides equal ⟹ triangles congruent ⟹ ∠A = ∠B

question: If cot θ = 7/8, evaluate: (i) [(1 + sin θ)(1 – sin θ)] / [(1 + cos θ)(1 – cos θ)] (ii) cot²θ
solution:

(1+cosθ)(1–cosθ) = 1 – cos²θ = sin²θ
So the expression = cos²θ/sin²θ = cot²θ = 49/64
(ii) cot²θ = (7/8)² = 49/64
steps: cot θ = 7/8 ⟹ cot²θ = 49/64
(i) Expression simplifies to cos²θ/sin²θ = cot²θ
Both (i) and (ii) equal 49/64

question: If 3 cot A = 4, check whether (1 – tan²A)/(1 + tan²A) = cos²A – sin²A or not.
solution:
3 cot A = 4 ⟹ cot A = 4/3 ⟹ tan A = 3/4
Take a right triangle with opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = √(9+16) = 5. So sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5.
LHS: (1 – tan²A)/(1 + tan²A) = (1 – 9/16)/(1 + 9/16) = (7/16)/(25/16) = 7/25
RHS: cos²A – sin²A = 16/25 – 9/25 = 7/25
Since LHS = RHS = 7/25, the given equation holds true for this value of A.
steps: 3 cot A = 4 ⟹ tan A = 3/4; use 3-4-5 triangle: sin A=3/5, cos A=4/5
RHS = 16/25–9/25 = 7/25; LHS = RHS, so the identity checks out

question:
In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if tan A = 1/√3, find the value of:
(i) sin A cos C + cos A sin C
(ii) cos A cos C – sin A sin C
solution:
Since tan A = 1/√3, ∠A = 30°. Since the triangle is right-angled at B, ∠A + ∠C = 90°, so ∠C = 60°.
sin A = 1/2, cos A = √3/2, sin C = √3/2, cos C = 1/2

(This is sin(A+C) = sin 90° = 1.)
(ii) cos A cos C – sin A sin C = (√3/2)(1/2) – (1/2)(√3/2) = √3/4 – √3/4 = 0
(This is cos(A+C) = cos 90° = 0.)
steps: tan A = 1/√3 ⟹ A=30°; since right angle at B, C = 90°–A = 60°
sin A=1/2, cos A=√3/2, sin C=√3/2, cos C=1/2
(i) sinAcosC+cosAsinC = sin(A+C) = sin90° = 1; (ii) cosAcosC–sinAsinC = cos(A+C) = cos90° = 0

question: In △PQR, right-angled at Q, PR + QR = 25 cm and PQ = 5 cm. Determine the values of sin P, cos P and tan P.
solution:
Let QR = x cm, so PR = (25 – x) cm.
By the Pythagoras theorem: PQ² + QR² = PR²
25 + x² = (25 – x)²
25 + x² = 625 – 50x + x²
25 = 625 – 50x
50x = 600
x = 12
So QR = 12 cm and PR = 25 – 12 = 13 cm.
sin P = (side opposite P)/hypotenuse = QR/PR = 12/13
cos P = (side adjacent to P)/hypotenuse = PQ/PR = 5/13
tan P = QR/PQ = 12/5
steps: Let QR = x, PR = 25–x; apply Pythagoras: PQ²+QR²=PR²
sin P = 12/13, cos P = 5/13, tan P = 12/5

question:
State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(i) The value of tan A is always less than 1.
(ii) sec A = 12/5 for some value of angle A.
(iii) cos A is the abbreviation used for the cosecant of angle A.
(iv) cot A is the product of cot and A.
(v) sin θ = 4/3 for some angle θ.
solution:
(i) False. tan A can be greater than 1; for example, tan 60° = √3 ≈ 1.73 > 1.
(ii) True. sec A ≥ 1 for any acute angle A, and 12/5 = 2.4 ≥ 1, so this is possible — for example, in a right triangle with hypotenuse 12 and adjacent side 5, the opposite side = √(144–25) = √119, which is a valid triangle.
(iii) False. cos A is the abbreviation for cosine of A; cosecant of A is written as cosec A.
(iv) False. cot A represents a single trigonometric ratio (cotangent of angle A), not the product of 'cot' and 'A' — just as sin A is not sin multiplied by A.
(v) False. Since sin θ = (side opposite θ)/(hypotenuse), and the hypotenuse is always the longest side of a right triangle, sin θ can never exceed 1. So sin θ = 4/3 (> 1) is not possible for any angle θ.
steps: (i) False — tan 60°=√3>1 is a counterexample
(ii) True — sec A≥1 always, and 12/5≥1 is achievable
(iii),(iv) False — notation misunderstandings; (v) False — sin θ ≤ 1 always

question:
Choose the correct option and justify your choice:
(i) 2 tan 30°/(1 + tan²30°) = (A) sin 60° (B) cos 60° (C) tan 60° (D) sin 30°
(ii) (1 – tan²45°)/(1 + tan²45°) = (A) tan 90° (B) 1 (C) sin 45° (D) 0
(iii) sin 2A = 2 sin A is true when A = (A) 0° (B) 30° (C) 45° (D) 60°
(iv) 2 tan 30°/(1 – tan²30°) = (A) cos 60° (B) sin 60° (C) tan 60° (D) sin 30°
solution:
(i) 2tan30°/(1+tan²30°) = 2(1/√3)/(1+1/3) = (2/√3)/(4/3) = (2/√3)×(3/4) = 6/(4√3) = √3/2 = sin 60°.
This matches the identity 2tanθ/(1+tan²θ) = sin 2θ, with θ=30°. Answer: (A) sin 60°
(ii) (1–tan²45°)/(1+tan²45°) = (1–1)/(1+1) = 0/2 = 0.
This matches cos 2θ = (1–tan²θ)/(1+tan²θ), with θ=45° giving cos90°=0. Answer: (D) 0
(iii) Testing A=0°: sin(2×0°)=sin0°=0, and 2sin0°=0. Both equal, so it holds. Testing A=30°,45°,60° gives unequal values (e.g., A=30°: sin60°=√3/2≈0.87 ≠ 2sin30°=1). Answer: (A) 0°
(iv) 2tan30°/(1–tan²30°) = 2(1/√3)/(1–1/3) = (2/√3)/(2/3) = (2/√3)×(3/2) = 3/√3 = √3 = tan 60°.
This matches the identity 2tanθ/(1–tan²θ) = tan 2θ, with θ=30°. Answer: (C) tan 60°

question:
State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(i) sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B
(ii) The value of sin θ increases as θ increases.
(iii) The value of cos θ increases as θ increases.
(iv) sin θ = cos θ for all values of θ.
(v) cot A is not defined for A = 0°.
solution:
(i) False. Counter-example: let A = B = 30°. sin(A+B) = sin60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, but sinA + sinB = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. Since 0.866 ≠ 1, the statement is false.
(ii) True. From the standard table of values, as θ increases from 0° to 90°, sin θ increases from 0 to 1 (0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1).
(iii) False. As θ increases from 0° to 90°, cos θ actually decreases from 1 to 0 (1, √3/2, 1/√2, 1/2, 0), not increases.
(iv) False. sin θ = cos θ only at θ = 45°, not for all θ. For example, at θ=30°, sin30°=1/2 but cos30°=√3/2, which are not equal.
(v) True. cot A = cos A/sin A, and sin 0° = 0. Division by zero is undefined, so cot 0° is not defined.
steps: (i) False — test A=B=30° gives sin60°≠sin30°+sin30°
(ii) True — sinθ increases 0→1 as θ goes 0°→90° (from the standard table)
(iii) False — cosθ decreases 1→0; (iv) False — true only at θ=45°; (v) True — cot0°=cos0°/sin0° undefined (division by 0)

question: Express the trigonometric ratios sin A, sec A and tan A in terms of cot A.
solution:
Using the identity cosec²A = 1 + cot²A:
cosec A = √(1 + cot²A)
sin A = 1/cosec A = 1/√(1 + cot²A)
tan A = 1/cot A
Using sec²A = 1 + tan²A = 1 + 1/cot²A = (cot²A + 1)/cot²A:
sec A = √(cot²A + 1)/cot A
steps: cosec²A = 1+cot²A ⟹ sin A = 1/√(1+cot²A)
tan A = 1/cot A
sec A = √(1+cot²A)/cot A

question: Write all the other trigonometric ratios of ∠A in terms of sec A.

Using sin²A = 1 – cos²A = 1 – 1/sec²A = (sec²A – 1)/sec²A:
sin A = √(sec²A – 1)/sec A
Using tan²A = sec²A – 1:
tan A = √(sec²A – 1)
cosec A = 1/sin A = sec A/√(sec²A – 1)
cot A = 1/tan A = 1/√(sec²A – 1)

sin A = √(sec²A–1)/sec A (from sin²A+cos²A=1)
tan A = √(sec²A–1); cosec A = secA/√(sec²A–1); cot A = 1/√(sec²A–1)

(iii) (sec A + tan A)(1 – sin A) = (A) sec A (B) sin A (C) cosec A (D) cos A
